ai.base_rate_used: Scenario page base rate: 0 downgrades in 36 recorded S&P actions on EU sovereigns tracked since 2014 when the outlook going in was stable (0%). Of those 36, 7 moved the outlook or watch to negative and 19 were affirmations. The page notes affirmations are under-recorded, so 0% is a lower bound. France is A+ with a stable outlook going in.

factors.text: S&P almost never cuts straight from a stable outlook. Its usual sequence is outlook to negative first, then a cut at a later review. The reference class shows 0 downgrades in 36 stable-outlook cases. That makes an outlook change, which resolves NO, the natural outlet for any worry.

The fiscal and political backdrop is getting worse. The HCFP calls the 1.0% growth assumption for 2027 optimistic and sees the deficit only falling from 5.4% to 5.0%. The budget is far from secure: markets give 57% (Polymarket) and 49% (Kalshi) to enactment in 2026, and 58% to the use of Article 49.3. The monthly OAT-Bund spread rose from 81.5 bp to 96.7 bp, though that series is degraded and up to five weeks old. This is enough to make a negative outlook plausible. A one-step cut on 27 Nov stays unlikely unless the government falls first.

There is no peer pressure from a fresh cut elsewhere: Moody's affirmed France on 23 Oct. The crowd agrees with a low number: Polymarket gives 7% to a Moody's or S&P downgrade by 30 Nov, and that is mostly S&P. The market is thin, however, so it confirms rather than informs.

ai.what_would_change_view: I would raise my estimate if a censure motion succeeds before 27 Nov, if the PLF 2027 revenue part is rejected at first reading so that a special law becomes the base case, or if the government raises its 2026 deficit estimate. Any of these could push S&P to skip the outlook step. A clean first-reading vote with no censure would push weight from affirm_negative to affirm_stable.
ai.most_likely_wrong: S&P could treat an already widening spread and a stalled budget as enough to cut without a negative outlook first, as agencies sometimes do with France. My view rests on a reference class with few such cases, and the budget timeline straddles the review date.

ai.base_rate_used: The scenario page's base rate is 19 of 21 budgets promulgated by 31 December (90.5%) across 2006-2026. I start there but give more weight to the subset since June 2022, when the government lost its majority, because it fits today's minority government better. The page lists that subset separately without a count. Its own analogs show the last two cycles, December 2024 and December 2025, both ended in a special law or a fallen government rather than a promulgated budget.

factors.text: The 90.5% base rate comes mostly from years with a working majority. Since 2024 the minority-government pattern has been a special law in December: the Barnier government fell in December 2024, and a special law replaced the budget in December 2025. A minority government still governs now.

The bill is hard to pass. It carries about 54 billion euros of consolidation, including a freeze of basic pensions and of civil-service pay. The fiscal watchdog (HCFP) says the spending path holds only if Parliament adopts every measure. With the presidential election in spring 2027, Mélenchon promising retirement at 60 and Le Pen near 45% in markets, opposition parties gain little by backing austerity.

There are still routes to YES. Kalshi gives 58% to Article 49.3 being used, a tool that has delivered budgets before when the government survived the censure vote. Article 47 also allows enactment by ordinance after the 10 December deadline, although it has never been used under the Fifth Republic.

ai.what_would_change_view: I would move up if the Socialists or LR publicly commit not to censure, or if a joint committee (CMP) agreement is reached in mid-December. I would move down if the National Assembly rejects the revenue part at first reading, if a censure motion gathers Socialist votes, or if the government signals a special law as its base case. An explicit government statement that it will use Article 47 would raise the ordinance branch.
ai.most_likely_wrong: I may be over-learning from two bad cycles. Before an election, opposition parties may prefer not to own a December crisis. The government may also have pre-negotiated abstentions, as with the 2025 pension-reform suspension deal, which would let 49.3 plus a survived censure vote deliver the budget on time. That is roughly what Polymarket's 57% implies.

ai.base_rate_used: The scenario page's base rate (final-poll leader won 4 of 4 run-offs; RMS poll error 5.78 pp) covers final polls only. There are no polls in the snapshot and the vote is six months away, so it cannot be applied directly. As a last resort I start from market prices: RN candidates combined are about 47 on Polymarket (Le Pen 45.1 plus Bardella 2.2) and about 48 on Kalshi (46.0 plus 1.8).

factors.text: Prediction markets have recently misread populist-right run-offs. In Brazil's 25 Oct 2026 run-off, Lula beat odds that gave Flávio Bolsonaro 80%. The prediction-market and poll-vs-market gauges are badged tested_no_lead, so a market price near 47 is a weak anchor. I shade slightly below it rather than adopt it.

The centre-right field is split (Lisnard 14.8, Philippe 10.5, Lagarde 7.4 on Polymarket), with no consolidation yet. A left candidate is also pushing costly pledges (retirement at 60). That raises the chance RN faces a weak or divisive run-off opponent, which supports RN being the single most likely winner.

Some press frames the US midterm rout as a crack in the populist right. These are unofficial headlines with no tested link to French voting, so they carry little weight. They mildly argue against treating RN as a near-coin-flip favourite.

ai.what_would_change_view: Second-round polls showing the RN candidate clearly ahead of the leading centre-right candidate would push me up. So would the field narrowing to a left candidate as RN's opponent. I would move down if one centre-right candidate consolidates and others withdraw by the March 2027 sponsorship deadline. A ruling on Le Pen's ineligibility matters mainly for who RN fields, not whether RN wins, since either candidate resolves YES.
ai.most_likely_wrong: I may be too sceptical of the market. If RN's run-off polling is now strong enough to overcome the traditional anti-RN vote in round two, the true probability could be above 50, and shading below the market would be a mistake.

ai.base_rate_used: The scenario page has no computed base rate; em-macro records no Brazilian fiscal-target revisions. I start from the two context cases on the page. In July 2015 the 2015 target was cut mid-year, and in April 2024 the 2025 target was cut through the budget guidelines bill. Neither change came in the first quarter of the target year. Formal cuts tend to arrive with mid-year reviews or the April guidelines bill, not by 31 March. From that I start at roughly two-in-three that the target and rule survive to 31 March, then adjust.

factors.text: The numbers make the +0.5% target hard to hit honestly. The IFI sees a potential 2027 deficit of 1.0% of GDP. The Focus median for the 2027 primary balance is -0.4%, below even the lower tolerance bound. The IFI says about R$35.7 billion of discretionary spending would have to be frozen. A big gap raises the temptation to change the target formally rather than freeze spending.

The question only asks whether the target and rule are formally unchanged, not whether they are met. The framework's legal deductions and exclusions (for example the R$33.8 billion consumption-tax compensation payment outside the spending cap) let a government keep the target on paper. That is the kept_exclusions branch, which counts as YES. The first bimonthly report in March usually freezes spending rather than proposes a new target.

Lula's re-election and the new term from 5 January widen the window for a reset: a new finance team, a December budget vote that could carry a bill changing the target, and markets already pricing loosening. The 10y rose 255bp on the day after the run-off, and the long fixed-rate and inflation-linked yields rose again this week. Dates before 31 March favour a quick formal change less than the April guidelines bill does, so this is a moderate pull down.

ai.what_would_change_view: Lower: a bill to change the 2027 target or the spending rule attached to the December budget vote, a new finance minister who calls the 0.5% target unrealistic, or the Focus 2027 primary median falling further. Higher: the budget voted without new exclusions and a finance minister in January who commits to the framework. On the market side, a fall in the DI Jan-29 proxy from 15.0% would suggest the market sees the framework as safer.
ai.most_likely_wrong: The crowd (bond markets after the run-off, the Focus median) may be right to expect an early formal change. A second-term government with no re-election at stake could rewrite the target in a December or January bill alongside the budget, rather than waiting for April. That would make the 2015 and 2024 timing a poor guide. The Focus primary-balance dispersion is untested as a signal, so I give it little weight either way.

ai.base_rate_used: The scenario page has a computed base rate, but it answers a different question: the final-poll leader won 3 of 3 Mexican midterms, with an RMS poll error of 4.12 pp. It says who wins, not whether the coalition clears 334 of 500 seats. The closer reference class is the page's note that in 2021 the governing coalition kept its majority but lost two-thirds. That is one case out of one where a coalition went into a midterm holding a supermajority, and it lost it. I start from a below-even prior and treat the 'most seats' markets as a floor for the majority branch only.

factors.text: Precedent: in the only recorded midterm where the governing coalition defended two-thirds (2021), it kept the majority but lost the supermajority. Two-thirds depends on vote share and the over-representation cap, so a small swing against the coalition is enough to fall below 334.

The election-year budget is tight. México Evalúa says the 3.9% deficit target rests on record tax collection and a sharp cut in support for Pemex. It expects any shortfall to fall on investment, health and education, the kind of squeeze that costs votes at the margin. Pemex capital contributions are cut 69.2% to 81.1 billion pesos. USMCA uncertainty adds to this: Kalshi gives 13% to a US withdrawal notice.

In 2024 the market and polls underestimated Morena's legislative strength. Sheinbaum led by 17pp and won by 33pp, and the supermajority surprised enough to move the peso 7.2% by day 5. Morena remains dominant: 89.2% and 86% to win the most seats. Together these keep the supermajority a live possibility rather than a tail.

ai.what_would_change_view: I would raise the probability if polls put the coalition above 55% of the vote, or if INE rulings ease the over-representation cap as in the 2024 dispute. I would lower it if coalition polls fall toward 45%, if PAN-PRI-MC alliances form in key districts, or if a US trade shock arrives before June. Candidate registration in January 2027 is the first hard signpost.
ai.most_likely_wrong: The likeliest error is underrating Morena again. Here the crowd's mistake runs the other way: the 'most seats' markets (89.2%, 86%) are read as comfort, yet they say nothing about two-thirds. Those markets are badged tested_no_lead, and the pollster house-effects gauge is untested. In 2024 the supermajority was exactly what a headline margin failed to capture. If the coalition's vote share holds near its 2024 level and seat allocation is generous, YES could be the base case and 35 too low.

As a last resort I start from market prices for the earlier, 2026 window: Kalshi gives 12% to a formal extension in 2026 (ks:KXUSMCAOUTCOMES-27-16Y) and Polymarket gives 7.5% (pm:2761052). I then allow a little extra for the longer window to 1 July 2027.

factors.text: Trade friction is still running case by case. USTR asked Mexico to review an alleged denial of workers' rights at Madobox on the same day it announced a memorandum at Industrias Tecnos. That looks like an administration using the review as ongoing leverage, not one ready to sign a long extension.

Markets put a US withdrawal notice in 2026 at 13%, slightly above the extension price, and a revised trilateral deal at 24%. The crowd sees renegotiation, not a clean renewal, as the more likely route. A YES also needs Canada to confirm in writing, which adds another point of failure.

Headlines after the US midterms describe a Trump defeat and lawmakers vowing to reverse tariffs. A weaker White House could make a face-saving extension at the July 2027 review somewhat more likely than the 2026 prices imply. The peso firmed over the week, but that is not specific to trade.

ai.what_would_change_view: USTR's consultation report (placeholder date 1 February 2027) recommending extension, or US tariffs on Mexican goods being cut, would push me up. A Federal Register withdrawal notice, or a US proposal for separate US-Mexico and US-Canada texts, would push me down towards zero. The date of the next bilateral round, now only a placeholder, is the first thing to watch.
ai.most_likely_wrong: Prediction-market prices carry little proven information: the pm and ks series are badged tested_no_lead, and these trade contracts are thin, a few thousand in volume. I lean on them for lack of a reference class. The single most likely way I am wrong is that a US administration weakened at the midterms decides a quick extension is an easy win before July 2027, which would make 15% too low.
